notes.h: The household as a financial unit
notes.b: A household is a group who share a home and make shared decisions about income, spending and saving. It is the basic financial unit of the economy, because everything the economy produces is ultimately bought, taxed or worked for by households.
points: Households spend on goods and services, which supports the businesses that supply them and the jobs those businesses provide.
Households pay taxes, which fund public services and State welfare payments.
Households buy property, and property purchases generate stamp duty, a tax that is income for the State.
Households supply the workforce: children who grow up in families become the future workers, so families that teach children money management also prepare the next generation.
Families usually run their finances independently, but they may need State aid, such as welfare payments or help from MABS, when income falls short of need.
notes.tip: In a 10-mark question on the household's role in the economy, cover spending that sustains jobs, tax and stamp duty, teaching money management, and that households are usually independent but may need State aid.

notes.b: Households receive money in different forms depending on whether, and how, their members work. The main sources are wages, salaries, pensions and State payments.
points: Wages: payment for hours worked or output, usually paid weekly or fortnightly, often for manual or hourly work. Because pay follows hours, a week with fewer hours means a smaller wage.
Salaries: a fixed annual amount paid in regular instalments, usually for non-manual or professional work, so the pay is the same each period.
Pensions: income after retirement from an employer's scheme, a personal pension fund or the State. Money paid into a pension while working is a voluntary deduction.
Social welfare allowances and benefits: payments made by the State to people who are unemployed, ill, disabled, caring, retired, widowed or raising children.
Other sources, in one line: profit from self-employment, rent from property, interest on savings, gifts and maintenance payments.
notes.tip: If asked to name three social welfare payments, any three valid names score, for example Child Benefit, Carer's Allowance and Fuel Allowance.

notes.h: Social factors that affect household income
notes.b: Two households with similar jobs can still have very different incomes. Age, gender, social class, culture and employment pattern all shape how much a household earns and what it must spend.
points: Age: income tends to rise with experience and promotion, then falls at retirement unless a pension has been arranged.
Age: teenagers can earn part-time income, which eases the financial strain on the family.

Gender: equal-pay law requires equal pay for the same work, but women are still under-represented in senior management, which men hold more of in many sectors. Women are also more likely to work part-time or take career breaks for caring.
Social class: low qualifications or early school leaving can lead to low pay or unemployment, while higher education widens access to better-paid work.
Culture: cultural attitudes shape whether women take paid work, which occupations are seen as suitable, and which spending priorities a household sets.
Employment pattern: the number of family members in paid work, and whether hours are full-time, part-time, job-sharing, flexible or seasonal, all change household income.
Disability, illness or addiction can reduce earning capacity and raise household costs, so income falls while spending needs rise.
notes.tip: Higher Level essays on this topic reward a reason for each factor, an example, and a consequence for the household. Treat employment pattern and the number of earners as extra factors beyond age, gender, social class and culture.

notes.b: The pay a person earns is not the pay they take home, because deductions are taken off first. Knowing which figure is which matters for both exams and household planning.
points: Gross income is income earned before any deductions are made.
Net income is take-home pay: gross income after deductions have been made.
Compulsory deductions from gross pay are PAYE, PRSI and USC. The law requires them, so the employee cannot choose to avoid them.

Voluntary deductions are chosen by the employee and include union subscriptions, pension contributions, additional voluntary contributions (AVCs, extra payments into a pension), health insurance, savings, social club fees and holiday fund payments.
Budgets are planned from net income, because net income is the money a household actually has to spend and save.
notes.tip: Students swap gross and net: gross is before deductions, net is after. Pension contributions are voluntary, so never list them as a compulsory deduction. For two compulsory and two voluntary deductions, use PAYE and PRSI, then pension contributions and health insurance.

notes.b: The three compulsory deductions each work differently and each pays for something different. Between them they take money from gross pay for the State.
points: PAYE (Pay As You Earn) is income tax deducted by the employer from each pay, based on the employee's earnings, and paid to the Revenue Commissioners (the State). It rises with income through a standard rate and a higher rate.
Revenue works out the employee's credits and rate band, and the employer uses these details to calculate the PAYE to deduct.
PAYE and USC go to the State to pay for public services such as health, education, roads and welfare.

PRSI (Pay Related Social Insurance) is a compulsory percentage of pay, so it is related to income. It is paid by the employee, through deduction, and separately by the employer, and it funds social insurance benefits.
Different PRSI classes exist, and self-employed people pay PRSI too. Employees earning below a set threshold are exempt from paying employee PRSI.
USC (Universal Social Charge) is a compulsory charge on gross income, calculated at rates that rise in bands as income rises. It is separate from income tax.
Employees with gross income below a set threshold are exempt from paying USC.
notes.tip: PRSI is a payment into social insurance, not a tax in the PAYE sense, and it is not private insurance. When explaining PAYE, say the employer deducts it, it goes to the State, it depends on earnings, and name two uses such as health and education.

notes.b: A tax credit lowers the tax bill itself, so it is worth the same as an equal amount of tax saved. It is not a reduction in the pay the tax is worked out on.
points: A tax credit reduces the amount of income tax a person has to pay. Examples are the personal credit and the employee (PAYE) credit.
Income tax is worked out on gross income first, and the person's tax credits are then subtracted from the tax calculated. A credit does not reduce income before tax is worked out.
Revenue works out the employee's credits and standard rate cut-off point (the income up to which the lower rate applies), and the employer uses them when deducting PAYE.
Tax credits do not reduce the USC, which is charged separately on gross income.
notes.tip: A tax credit reduces the tax owed, not gross income, and it does not reduce USC. Say credits are subtracted after the tax has been calculated.

notes.h: Social insurance and social assistance payments
notes.b: The State pays welfare in two ways. One is earned through PRSI contributions; the other is paid from taxes to people who do not qualify for the first, and it checks their means.
points: Social insurance payments are paid to people who have made the minimum PRSI contributions, so the person has earned them, and they are not means tested.
Examples of social insurance payments: Jobseeker's Benefit, Illness Benefit, Maternity Benefit, Carer's Benefit and the contributory State pension.
Social assistance payments are paid from taxes to people whose PRSI contributions are insufficient to qualify for social insurance payments, and they are means tested.

Examples of social assistance payments: Jobseeker's Allowance, Disability Allowance, Carer's Allowance and the non-contributory State pension. Carer's Benefit is the PRSI-based alternative to Carer's Allowance.
A means test assesses the claimant's income and capital (usually including a partner's) against a set limit. The payment is reduced or refused as means rise above it.
notes.tip: Social insurance means contributions and no means test; social assistance means a means test. Give one named example of each. Disability Allowance is social assistance, never social insurance.

notes.b: Some payments follow neither pattern exactly. A universal payment is paid to everyone who meets one condition, without a means test or a contribution record.
points: Child Benefit: a monthly universal payment for each qualifying child. It is not means tested and does not depend on PRSI contributions.
Working Family Payment: a weekly payment to employees on low pay who have children, and means tested against a family-size income limit. It replaced the name Family Income Supplement.
Supplementary Welfare Allowance: means tested, and paid to people whose means cannot meet their basic needs or those of their dependants.
Supplementary Welfare Allowance can also be a temporary payment for people awaiting another benefit while their claim is being processed.
Maternity Benefit: a social insurance payment for employees on maternity leave.
Other payments a student may name: Carer's Allowance, Disability Allowance, Back to School Clothing and Footwear Allowance and Fuel Allowance.
notes.tip: Short items test Child Benefit as universal, Working Family Payment as for low-paid employees with children, and Supplementary Welfare Allowance as means tested. Child Benefit is neither a contribution-based nor a means-tested payment.

notes.b: There are two State pensions for older people, and the difference between them is the same as the difference between social insurance and social assistance.
points: The contributory State pension (formerly called the old age pension) is based on the claimant's record of PRSI contributions.
The contributory pension is not means tested, so other income does not normally remove entitlement to it.
The non-contributory State pension is means-tested social assistance for an older person who lacks enough PRSI contributions.
Eligibility for the non-contributory pension depends on means and on residence conditions, including habitual residence in the State (a settled, normal home there).
notes.tip: Contrast the two by the PRSI record and no means test, against a means test. Never call the non-contributory pension free: it is means tested.

keyTerms.definition: Income earned before any deductions are made.
Take-home pay: gross income after compulsory and voluntary deductions have been made.
Pay As You Earn, the income tax deducted from wages by the employer and paid to the State.
Pay Related Social Insurance, a compulsory percentage of pay shared by employer and employee to fund social insurance benefits.
Universal Social Charge, a compulsory charge on gross income that rises with income.
An amount deducted from the income tax a person owes, which reduces the tax paid.
A State payment available to people who have made the minimum PRSI contributions, and not dependent on means.
A means-tested State payment for people whose PRSI contributions are insufficient for social insurance payments.
An assessment of a claimant's income against a set limit to decide whether a payment is made and how much.

factCards.definition: The contributory pension, based on PRSI contributions and not means tested, and the non-contributory pension, which is means-tested social assistance.
Social insurance is based on PRSI contributions and is not means tested; social assistance is means tested and for people with insufficient PRSI contributions.
Child Benefit, paid for each qualifying child and not means tested.

factCards.term: Working Family Payment: who it helps
factCards.definition: Employees on low pay who have children; it is means tested.

factCards.term: Two features of Supplementary Welfare Allowance
factCards.definition: It is means tested, and it can be paid temporarily to people awaiting another benefit.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between gross income and net income, and name two compulsory deductions made from gross pay.
questions.model: Gross income is income earned before any deductions are made. Net income is take-home pay, the amount left after deductions have been made. Two compulsory deductions: PAYE, which is income tax deducted by the employer; PRSI, which is pay-related social insurance paid by employer and employee to fund social welfare benefits. USC, the universal social charge on gross income, is also acceptable.

questions.prompt: Analyse the factors that affect household income, and explain the difference between social insurance payments and social assistance payments, giving one named example of each.
questions.model: Age: income rises with experience and promotion and falls at retirement unless a pension is in place; teenagers may earn part-time income. Gender: equal-pay law applies, but senior management can remain male-dominated. Social class: low qualifications or early school leaving limit pay and job options, while higher education widens them. Culture: shapes whether women take paid work and what the household prioritises. Employment pattern: number of family members working, full-time, part-time, job-sharing, flexible or seasonal hours. Disability or addiction: reduces earning capacity and raises costs. Social insurance payments: based on the minimum PRSI contributions, not means tested; example Jobseeker's Benefit or Illness Benefit. Social assistance payments: for people with insufficient PRSI contributions, means tested; example Jobseeker's Allowance or Carer's Allowance.
